Where Hennepin County records a deed

The Hennepin County Recorder and Registrar of Titles records deeds, mortgages, assignments, releases and satisfactions. The office is on the 7th floor of the A-tower at the Government Center, 300 South 6th Street in Minneapolis. It also takes military separations and tax liens. Call 612-348-5139 or write to recordinginfo@hennepin.us.

About 45% of the land in this county is registered as Torrens, so the recorder handles a mix of abstract and Torrens parcels. That mix shapes how a sale gets recorded, and it is the first thing to learn about a house you are selling.

Ways to get a document recorded

There are four routes, and different filers are steered to different ones.

  • In person by appointment, offered between 8:30 a.m. and 3:30 p.m. each business day. A walk-in goes on a wait list and is helped when staff are free. Visitors clear security screening on the Skyway level first.
  • eRecording, the preferred method for title companies, lenders, law firms and other commercial filers. Documents are recorded within 1 to 3 days, and the original never leaves your hands.
  • Online through the Virtual Recorder site, open to the general public. You register, build a package, and pay by card or eCheck. Each order carries a $3 service fee and is reviewed for recordability before you pay, then recorded in 1 to 3 business days.
  • By mail to County Recorder/Registrar of Titles, Attn: Document recording, 300 S Sixth St, MC 074, Minneapolis, MN 55487. Originals are returned within 1 to 2 weeks of receipt.

If a statutory deadline is close, call the office and ask which option fits.

Recording fees

An abstract or Torrens document costs $46 to record, and one check made out to Hennepin County Recorder can cover both the recording fee and any tax. The fees come from Minnesota Statutes 357.18. These are the charges a seller or buyer is most likely to meet.

Selected Hennepin County recorder fees
Document or serviceFee
Abstract or Torrens document$46
Additional Torrens certificate$20 each
Assignment or satisfaction (abstract)$46, plus $10 for each reference over four
Well disclosure certificate$54
Conservation fee on taxed instruments$5
State tax lien release$30
Extra copies at filing$2
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Hennepin County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Taxes and paperwork that go with a deed

A transfer deed needs more than a signature. The recording checklist calls for these items:

  • State deed tax of .0034 of the net consideration, figured with the online deed tax calculator. For a transfer of $3,000 or less the tax is $1.70, and the deed should carry the words "Total consideration for this transfer is $3,000 or less."
  • An electronic certificate of real estate value, or eCRV, with its number on the first page, for any deed over $3,000. Paper CRVs cause the package to be rejected.
  • A $5 agricultural conservation fee on any deed where state deed tax is due.
  • A "Send Tax Statements to" line with the name and address of every buyer.
  • A well statement, or a well disclosure certificate with its $54 fee.
  • Grantor marital status, a full legal description, a drafter name and address, and a notary block with seal and commission expiration.

A mortgage carries mortgage registry tax at .0024 of the amount. A contract for deed needs a well statement and an eCRV but no deed tax.

Does unpaid tax block recording?

Yes. Properties with delinquent taxes may not be transferred, under Minnesota Statutes 272.12. That section directs the auditor to check for delinquent tax, certify it, and mark the deed once it is paid or none is owed. The recorder cannot accept the deed without that mark, with exceptions the statute lists, such as deeds of distribution in probate and transfer on death deeds.

As a seller, get the tax payoff before the closing date so the title company can pay it from proceeds and the deed is not rejected. A cash buyer does not change this step: the auditor's check applies to every transfer. The property tax office at 612-348-3011 can quote what is owed on a parcel.

Why a package gets rejected

Staff review a document only for the elements Minnesota law requires, so a package comes back when one is missing. Common reasons:

  • No date or signature, or an incomplete legal description.
  • No drafted-by statement with the drafter's name and address.
  • A notary acknowledgment missing the date, a legible seal, the signature or the commission expiration date. An individual acknowledgment also needs the signer's name and marital status, and a corporate one the business name and the signer's title.
  • Strikeouts, line throughs, whiteout, correction tape or staple removal on the original.
  • No eCRV number on page one of a deed over $3,000.

The office cannot supply forms, help fill them out or give legal advice. For that, try Law Help MN, the Volunteer Lawyers Network or the district court self-help centers. The Minnesota Department of Commerce offers free templates meant to cut rejections.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Hennepin County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Torrens or abstract

Torrens land has been registered by order of the District Court or the Examiner of Titles. It has a certificate of title listing the owner, the legal description and every lien, and a new certificate is issued at each sale, much like a car title. Abstract property has no certificate, so an attorney or title company has to produce a report of owners and liens.

The property information search shows which kind a parcel is. An owner can get a free electronic copy of a deed or certificate of title by emailing recordsrequest@hennepin.us with the address or property identification number. A Torrens owner can also call 612-348-5139 for a free copy.

After closing

An attorney or title company normally does the recording, though a seller or buyer can do it. Once recorded, the county images and indexes the document, returns the original, and updates the taxpayer name and address from the deed. In most cases the document recorded first has priority.

Buyers can register the parcel with Property Watch, a free service that sends an email whenever a document is recorded against it. It does not prevent fraud, but it flags a recording nobody expected. If a joint owner has died, the survivor records an Affidavit of Survivorship with a certified death certificate. An owner who finds an old racial covenant in the chain of title can discharge it, and for abstract property there is no fee to record that disavowal.

Frequently asked questions

How much does the Hennepin County recorder charge for a deed?

$46 per abstract or Torrens document, plus a $5 conservation fee when state deed tax is paid, plus the deed tax itself. Checks go to Hennepin County Recorder, and one check can cover both fee and tax.

Can I record a deed online in Hennepin County without a title company?

Yes. The public can use the Virtual Recorder site after registering. Orders carry a $3 service fee, are checked for recordability before payment, and are recorded within 1 to 3 business days of payment.

How long does Hennepin County take to record mailed documents?

Originals mailed in are recorded and returned within 1 to 2 weeks of the county receiving them. eRecording from a vendor takes 1 to 3 days.

What is the Hennepin County deed tax rate?

State deed tax is .0034 of net consideration, with a flat $1.70 when the price is $3,000 or less. Use the county's online calculator for the exact amount.

Where is the Hennepin County recorder's office?

It is on the 7th floor of the A-tower at the Hennepin County Government Center, 300 South 6th Street, Minneapolis, MN 55487. Call 612-348-5139 or write recordinginfo@hennepin.us.

Selling in Ramsey County?

Where Ramsey County records a deed

Deeds, mortgages and other land documents go to the Ramsey County Recorder and Registrar of Titles Office in the Plato Building, 90 Plato Blvd. West, Saint Paul, MN 55107. The building opens Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. and closes on weekends and county holidays. Call 651-266-2050 with recording questions.

This is where the county's official land records are kept, and staff will retrieve and copy them for individuals and businesses. Know two things before closing day, whether you are selling through an agent or handling the paperwork yourself. Staff do not help complete legal forms, and once a document is recorded it stays on the record for good. A later change means recording a new document.

The Plato Building also holds the County Assessor, Property Tax Services, the Examiner of Titles and the tax-forfeited land office, so a payoff request, an examiner approval and a recording can often be handled on one trip.

The county has two kinds of land record, and a seller should know which one applies to the house.

Is your house Torrens or abstract?

Every parcel is either abstract or Torrens. Torrens land has been registered by order of the District Court or the Examiner of Titles, and the owner holds a certificate of title that names the owner, describes the land and lists every encumbrance, lien and interest that affects it. Abstract land has no certificate; its history is the chain of recorded documents.

The distinction changes the paperwork. A deed for a Torrens parcel is registered with the Registrar of Titles, and the Examiner of Titles, an appointed attorney, acts as legal adviser to the Registrar. Certain documents need an Examiner's certificate before they can be recorded, such as a trustee's deed or a probate conveyance. A request goes by email as separate PDF scans, the fee is generally $150 when all the land sits on a single certificate, and approval usually takes two to three business days. The fee is owed even if the closing never happens.

A document that covers both abstract and Torrens land can be handled two ways: send two sets of originals with two fee payments, one to the Recorder and one to the Registrar, or send one set to one side first and then submit the recorded copy, with its cover page showing the document number and taxes paid, to the other side.

Old entries on a certificate of title can be cleaned up. The Examiner publishes a deletion table describing when items drop off a certificate and accepts requests to delete recitals or memorials that no longer apply. A seller with a Torrens parcel and a stale entry should raise it before the closing date.

Recording fees

Minnesota Statutes 357.18 caps the fee for indexing and recording a deed or similar instrument at $46, and Ramsey County charges that amount. The 2026 and 2027 schedule lists these charges:

Selected Ramsey County recorder fees
Recorder serviceFee
Recording a document (abstract)$46
Document transferring a Torrens certificate$46
Multiple satisfaction or assignment$46
Exchange certificate (Torrens)$20
Well disclosure statement$50
State tax lien release$30
Certified copy$10
Non-certified copy or duplicate original$2

The county's notary service adds $5 for each notarial certificate. The signer must appear in person with ID, and the property must be in Ramsey County. These recording charges are separate from state deed tax and from any examiner fee.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Ramsey County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What taxes and attachments go with a deed?

A deed here comes with more than a signature and a fee. Expect these attachments and charges:

  • State deed tax, due when the deed is presented. Under 287.21 it is $1.65 when the price is $3,000 or less and .0033 of the net consideration above that.
  • A certificate of value filed with the county auditor for any sale over $3,000, required by 272.115. The filing also matters for homestead: the buyer must apply to keep that status for the next assessment year.
  • A well disclosure certificate with the $50 fee, or one of two statements on the deed. The first says the seller knows of no wells on the property. The second says the wells have not changed since the last certificate on file.
  • The auditor's note that no delinquent taxes are owed and transfer has been entered. Without it, 272.12 tells the recorder or registrar to refuse most deeds.

Contracts for deed need the well disclosure as well. The form you choose may change the tax result, so confirm it with your title company before you sign.

What to clear up before the deed is recorded

Start with the tax side. If any balance is open, call Delinquent Tax Information at 651-266-2002 for a payoff, and check that the current installment shows up on the closing statement.

Next, look at liens. The Recorder files several kinds:

  • Mechanics and attorney liens
  • Medical and hospital liens
  • Court judgment liens
  • Federal and state tax liens

Most are removed by recording a satisfaction, release, termination or cancellation, and both the lien and its release remain part of the permanent record. Liens themselves do not appear on credit reports, though the underlying loan still can.

Finally, if a document has a mistake, most corrective documents can be recorded if they carry new signatures and acknowledgments plus a correction statement on the face of the paper. Check with a title company or attorney before you sign. Recorder staff cannot give legal advice or hand out blank forms. Minnesota Uniform Conveyancing Blanks is a suggested source.

A cash sale skips the lender's payoff and release, but the same tax certification and recording steps still apply. At the counter, hand over your ID, the signed deed, the certificate of value and the well disclosure, then have staff total the charges before you pay.

Looking up and copying land records

Land records from the Recorder and the Registrar of Titles can be searched online through RecordEASE, which works on a subscription basis, or in person at the Property Records Resource Center. The county posts document posting dates so you can see how current the indexing is. Check that date before you rely on a search, since a document recorded this week may not be indexed yet.

Owners of older homes should also know about historic racial covenants. The county records a resolution in the tract index giving notice that such covenants are unenforceable and of no legal effect. An owner who wants to formally discharge one can record an affidavit, and residents are exempt from the filing fee.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Ramsey County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

How much does it cost to record a deed in Ramsey County?

The recording fee is $46 for a document, matching the state cap. A well disclosure statement adds $50 if you file the certificate. State deed tax is separate and is .0033 of net consideration on a sale over $3,000.

How do I reach the Ramsey County Recorder?

Phone 651-266-2050, or visit the Plato Building in Saint Paul, 90 Plato Blvd. West, on weekdays between 8 a.m. and 4:30 p.m.

Does Ramsey County notarize documents for real estate sales?

Yes, for documents about real property in Ramsey County. Each notarial certificate costs $5, and the signer must be there in person with valid ID.

Will the Ramsey County Recorder give me a blank deed form?

No. Staff cannot provide forms, advise on which forms you need, or help you fill them out. Ask an attorney, a title company or a legal form vendor, or look at Minnesota Uniform Conveyancing Blanks.

Can a mistake in a recorded Ramsey County deed be fixed?

Often, yes. Most corrective documents can be recorded when they carry new signatures and acknowledgments and note the correction on the document itself. The original record stays in place.

Dakota County, MN County Recorder: Recording a Deed, Fees and Transfer Tax

Cash Home Buyers in Minnesota

  • Dakota County, MN County Recorder: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Dakota County, MN County Recorder sale

Selling in Dakota County? Get a Cash Offer

We buy Dakota County houses as-is and reply with a written cash offer.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Dakota County?
We buy Dakota County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

Where to record a deed

Deeds, mortgages and liens are recorded at Property Taxation & Records, inside the Administration Center at 1590 Highway 55 in Hastings. This is the only place documents are accepted for recording, by appointment or by mail. The Western and Northern Service Centers take tax payments but not recordings.

Questions go to 651-438-4597 or records@co.dakota.mn.us. A mailed filing goes to Attn: Document Recording and should include a cover letter listing what is enclosed, a self-addressed stamped envelope, the fees and a phone number. Originals come back to the sender in one to two weeks.

Recording fees and transfer taxes

Recording fees are set by the state. The $46 charge for indexing and recording a deed or other instrument comes from Minnesota Statutes section 357.18, which divides it into $10.50 for the state general fund, $10 for the county technology fund and $25.50 for the county general fund. Fees are due at filing.

Dakota County recorder fees and transfer taxes
ChargeAmount
Abstract document or Torrens memorial$46
Plat or registered land survey$56
Conservation fee$5
Well disclosure certificate$50
Extra copy submitted at filing$2
Deed taxPurchase price times .0033 (minimum $1.65)
Mortgage registration taxMortgage amount times .0023

Pay with cash, check or card. Make checks out to Dakota County Property Taxation & Records. Cards add a 2.49% service charge on recordings but nothing on copy requests.

Deed tax on a sale

State deed tax is the purchase price multiplied by .0033. Section 287.21 applies that rate to the net consideration when the price, leaving out liens that stay on the property, is above $3,000. At $3,000 or less the tax is a flat $1.65.

The tax is due when the deed is presented. For a transfer worth $3,000 or less, enclose $1.65 and write "Total consideration for this transfer is $3,000 or less" on the deed. Above that amount an electronic certificate of real estate value is required under section 272.115, and it must be on file before the next homestead classification can apply to the buyer.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Dakota County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What a deed must contain

Documents here follow Minnesota Statutes section 507.093. Each one must be dated and signed, carry a complete notary acknowledgment, give the full legal description (not the tax description), attach any exhibits it mentions, and include a drafting statement and the filing fee. White-out is not accepted.

  • The deed tax is paid and the certificate of real estate value is complete.
  • The buyer's name and address appear so later tax statements reach the right person.
  • Delinquent taxes are paid, and current taxes too if the parcel is being split.
  • A married seller is joined by the spouse, who signs and is acknowledged as grantor.
  • Well information is included: a certificate with the $50 fee, or one of the two statements printed on the county recording page.
  • The $5 agricultural conservation fee is paid on transfers and mortgages.

A deed that completes a contract for deed needs a well statement signed by the buyers or a well certificate.

Why a document comes back

The recorder returns documents unrecorded for a short list of reasons, and each can be caught with a check before you mail or bring the package in.

  • Delinquent real estate tax is owed on the parcel.
  • The drafting statement is missing.
  • The deed tax or mortgage registration tax is wrong.
  • The legal description is incorrect or looks questionable next to county records.
  • The certificate of real estate value is missing or incomplete.
  • The mailing name and address for future tax statements is left out.
  • The notary acknowledgment is incomplete.
  • The recording fee is wrong, or a transfer lacks well information.

Section 272.12 also requires the auditor to confirm no delinquent tax exists. The deed then carries the note "no delinquent taxes and transfer entered" before the recorder can accept it. Fixing an error later takes a correction document with new signatures, new acknowledgments and a correction statement.

Abstract and Torrens land

Minnesota runs two land record systems. Most Dakota County property is Abstract, so a title company searches the records for anything touching the parcel when it sells. Torrens property has a Certificate of Title that works as conclusive proof of ownership, with some exceptions. Torrens work costs more: $20 for each additional Torrens memorial, $46 for the first certificate canceled and issued on a transfer, and $40 for each additional certificate.

To learn which system applies to a parcel, open the Property Information Search, enter the parcel ID or house number, and use the map layer icon. An owner can convert Abstract land to Torrens through land registration.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Dakota County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Recording a sale, step by step

For a typical sale the title company or attorney handles recording, but a seller who files directly can follow this order. First, confirm with Property Taxation & Records that no delinquent tax is open on the parcel. Second, complete the deed with the full legal description, drafting statement, notary block and the buyer's mailing address. Third, finish the electronic certificate of real estate value if the price is above $3,000. Fourth, calculate deed tax, add the $46 recording fee, the $5 conservation fee and any $50 well certificate, and write one check or plan to pay by card. Fifth, book an appointment in Hastings or mail the package with a stamped return envelope.

Most addresses in the county change hands slowly, and the office keeps records for 185,931 housing units, so a package that follows this checklist moves through without trouble. If something is wrong, the office returns the document with the reason, you fix it, and you file again, which is why checking the list first saves a round trip of one to two weeks.

Searching records online

The county's Property Information Search is free and shows tax, valuation and parcel data from a parcel ID, house number or address. RecordEASE is the paid tool for recorded documents, searched by legal description, grantor, grantee or document type.

Occasional users pay $5 a session, $1 per search and $2 to view a document. Subscribers pay $30 a month, $0.50 per search and $1.50 per document, and need an escrow account. Certificates of title cost $3 or $2.50 each. A former service member who recorded a discharge in the county can ask for a free DD214 copy. Most liens can be removed by filing a satisfaction, which stays on record permanently.

Frequently asked questions

Can I record a Dakota County deed at the Western or Northern Service Center?

No. Property documents are recorded only at the Property Taxation and Records office in the Administration Center in Hastings. You can also mail them to 1590 Highway 55, Hastings, MN 55033.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Dakota County?

The recording fee is $46 per document. Add the $5 conservation fee on transfers, the $50 well certificate if needed, and state deed tax of .0033 times the price. A card adds 2.49%.

Do I need a certificate of real estate value in Dakota County?

Yes when the price is above $3,000: you complete an electronic certificate of real estate value. For $3,000 or less none is needed, but you enclose $1.65 and add the required statement to the deed.

How long until the Dakota County recorder returns my original deed?

Originals are mailed back within one to two weeks. Include a self-addressed stamped envelope with a mailed filing. Questions go to 651-438-4597.

Does Dakota County help fill out a deed form?

No. The office does not help complete legal forms. Minnesota uniform conveyance forms are on the Department of Commerce site, and a seller who wants a deed drafted should ask a title company or attorney.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Carver County?

Where to record a deed

Deeds for Carver County land are recorded by the Land Records & Vitals office at 600 East 4th Street in Chaska, the county seat. Office hours run weekdays, 8:00am to 4:30pm, with closures on government holidays. For land records questions, call (952) 361-1930 or write to recorders@carvercountymn.gov.

The office handles more than deeds: conveyances, parcel splits and combinations, annexations, plats, mortgage registration tax, state deed tax, conservation fee collection and federal, state and county tax liens. Once a document is recorded it becomes a permanent record and cannot be changed or removed, so have the title company or an attorney check the deed before you sign.

Work out the sequence ahead of closing day, and leave a few days for fixes: have the deed drafted, signed and notarized, confirm the legal description matches your title commitment, complete the certificate of value and well disclosure, and then submit the package with payment. If a title company is closing your sale, it usually handles those steps and files the deed electronically, so ask for a copy of the recorded document afterward. Keep it with your closing papers, because a lender, an estate attorney or a later buyer may ask to see it.

Staff will not hand you a blank deed or tell you how to fill one in. Blank forms come from the Minnesota Department of Commerce, which publishes the Uniform Conveyancing Forms.

What the recorder checks on a deed

A deed that comes back unrecorded is usually missing one of a handful of items. The recording requirements page lists them:

  • A full legal description. The abbreviated one on your tax statement will not do.
  • A complete acknowledgment showing the state and county of signing, the date, the notary's seal, signature and commission expiration date, and each signer's marital status. If a company signs, add the business name plus the signer's name and title.
  • A drafted-by statement with a name and address, and a send-tax-statement-to name and address.
  • A Certificate of Real Estate Value when the price is over $3,000.
  • Well information whenever an eCRV is filed, and a subsurface sewage treatment system disclosure on every transfer.

Paper deeds need ink signatures from the parties and the notary, as required by Minn. Stat. 507.24. No correction fluid. To fix a typo, draw one line or a row of Xs through the error, type the right text and have the parties initial the change.

Recording fees

Indexing and recording a deed carries a $46 statutory charge, set by Minn. Stat. 357.18. Of that, $10.50 goes to the state general fund, $10 to the county technology fund and $25.50 to the county general fund.

State law also bars counties from adding their own charges for handling, mailing, certifying that no delinquent taxes are owed, or collecting deed tax and the conservation fee (357.182). These are the line items that can appear on a deed closing.

Charges that can apply when a deed is recorded in Carver County
ChargeAmount
Recording fee, deed$46
Certified copy$10
State deed tax, sale over $3,0000.33% of net consideration
State deed tax, price $3,000 or less$1.65
Agriculture conservation fee$5 per transaction on a deed subject to tax
Well disclosure certificate$54
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Carver County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How deed tax is figured

Above $3,000, deed tax equals 0.0033 times net consideration, meaning the price minus any lien that remains on the property after the sale. A deed showing no price, or $3,000 or less, pays $1.65. Payment is due at the moment the deed is submitted. The closing statement shows who covers it, so read that line before you sign.

The statute names some transfers as designated transfers, and those pay only the $1.65 minimum. If you are moving title to a relative or an entity, ask an attorney whether the label fits before you count on it.

Abstract and Torrens property

The state allows two land record systems, and the typical Carver County parcel sits under the Abstract system. Abstract land is proven through a title search of every recorded document that touches it. Torrens land has a Certificate of Title that serves as close to conclusive proof of ownership, and it folds the parcel's records into one document. An owner can convert Abstract land to Torrens through land registration.

Each system has its own recording rules, so tell the title company which kind of parcel you are selling. A document that covers both Abstract and Torrens land cannot be eRecorded at this time.

Recording time and eRecording

Statute 357.182 sets the turnaround: ten business days to record, index and return a recordable instrument. A county may take up to five more business days for documents that need a no-delinquent-tax certification or payment of deed tax, mortgage registry tax or the conservation fee. Electronically recorded instruments must come back within five business days of receipt in recordable form.

Carver County calls eRecording its preferred method and accepts nearly every Abstract or Torrens document type that way. Title companies, lenders and law firms sign up through one of the county's Trusted Submitters. A full eRecording also uses the electronic certificate of real estate value (eCRV) and the electronic well disclosure certificate (eWell).

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Carver County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Homestead status after a sale

With the deed, the certificate of value travels to the county auditor, then on to the assessor and the Department of Revenue. Under Minn. Stat. 272.115, a sold property loses its homestead classification for the next assessment year unless the buyer applies and qualifies. If a certificate of value was required but never filed, homestead treatment is barred.

The county assessor (952-361-1960, assessment@carvercountymn.gov) handles homestead applications. A new owner, a trust transfer, a name change or an added or removed owner each calls for a new application.

A house with deferred repairs, a tenant or an inherited title follows the same recording steps as a move-in-ready listing. A cash sale skips lender paperwork, but the deed, the certificate of value and the tax all still go through the Chaska office.

Local market context

Carver County borders Hennepin County in the Minneapolis-St. Paul-Bloomington metropolitan area. Population is 114,379, and builders pulled 960 permits in 2025. The cities are Carver, Chanhassen, Chaska, Cologne, Hamburg, Mayer, New Germany, Norwood Young America, Victoria, Waconia and Watertown.

  • Median owner-occupied home value: $453,600
  • Owner-occupied rate: 81.5%
  • Median gross rent: $1,514

Frequently asked questions

Where do I take a deed in Chaska?

The Land Records & Vitals office at 600 East 4th Street, Chaska, MN 55318. It keeps weekday hours from 8:00am to 4:30pm and shuts for government holidays. Call (952) 361-1930 to reach it.

What does Carver County charge to file a deed?

The statutory fee is $46 for indexing and recording a deed. Add the $5 agriculture conservation fee on a taxable deed, the state deed tax and, where a well certificate is needed, the $54 well fee.

Does Carver County require a notary on a deed?

Yes. A paper deed needs original signatures and a complete acknowledgment that shows the venue, date, notary seal and signature, and the notary's commission expiration date. Electronic deeds follow the state's electronic recording standards.

Can a Carver County deed be recorded online?

Yes, for nearly all Abstract and Torrens documents, through one of the county's Trusted Submitters such as a title company. Documents that mix Abstract and Torrens land cannot be eRecorded yet.

Who pays the state deed tax?

The tax is due on the deed presented for recording, and the statute does not assign it to a party. The sales contract and closing statement decide that, so ask the closing agent before you sign.

Where to record a deed

The County Recorder, who also serves as Registrar of Titles, takes in every deed for land in Rice County. The office is in the Government Services Building, 320 Third St. NW, Faribault. The phone number is 507-332-6114.

The Recorder files documents for both Abstract and Torrens property, plus plats, federal and state tax liens, military discharges and more than 300 other document types. Staff accept, review, receipt, index and scan each filing, and they take paper or electronic submissions. The office will not give legal advice or help prepare documents, so a closing agent or attorney should draft the deed.

Is your property Abstract or Torrens?

Most Rice County property is Abstract, but confirm that before a sale. Minnesota has two recording systems, and the paperwork differs between them.

With Abstract title, an abstract is a condensed history of every deed, mortgage and other document touching the land, and an attorney or title insurer reviews it. With Torrens title, a court directs issuance of a certificate of title, and the certificate itself is the title. The Recorder acts as Registrar of Titles and works with the Examiner of Titles, who advises the registrar. In Rice County the Examiner is Debbie Korman at 507-334-5534, 504 Central Ave. N, P.O. Box 716, Faribault.

The county posts a Torrens property list, but it is partial. For any single parcel, run a title search of the land records to learn which system applies.

How to get a document recorded

Bring or mail a paper original to the Recorder, or send it electronically through one of the e-recording partners:

  • Simplifile, 800-460-5657.
  • CSCGlobal, 866-652-0111.
  • eRecording Partners (GOePN), 888-325-3365.
  • Indecomm Global Services, 877-272-5250.
  • Hopdox, 385-501-5103.

Recording reproduces the document and returns the original to whoever presented it. Filing means the office keeps the original. Deeds and mortgage releases are recorded. The research area is open to the public during business hours, there is no charge to look, and printed copies of recorded documents run $1.00 per page.

For online research, the Recorder has scanned 1,166 plats, 789,492 Abstract documents and 60,375 Torrens documents into LandShark. Access costs $50 a month plus $2 per document, with a $50 set-up fee.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Rice County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Recording fees

Minnesota Statutes section 357.18 caps recorder fees, and Rice County follows that schedule. Write recorder fees on one check made out to Rice County. Deed tax and mortgage registry tax go on a separate check, because the Property Tax & Elections department processes the tax.

Rice County Recorder charges
ServiceCharge
Indexing and recording a deed or other instrument$46
Document with multiple assignments or releases$46, plus $10 for each citation over four
Certified copy of a record$10
Recording a plat$56
Copy of an official plat$10, plus $5 to certify
Printed copy of a recorded page$1.00 per page

Deed tax and required certificates

State deed tax comes from section 287.21. When the net consideration is more than $3,000 the tax is .0033 of it. When it is $3,000 or less, or the transfer has no consideration, the tax is $1.65. Payment is due when the deed is handed in.

Several other items go in with the deed:

  • A certificate of value (CRV) for any sale above $3,000, listing the Social Security or employer number of every grantor and grantee under section 272.115.
  • A well disclosure statement or certificate on a transfer for more than $3,000, on the Minnesota Department of Health form.
  • A drafting statement with the full name and address of the person who prepared the document.
  • The grantor's marital status, and the spouse's signature where required.
  • A notary acknowledgment that meets Minnesota Statutes section 359.03.

Gather all five before you send the package. A missing item is the most common reason a deed comes back.

Why the Recorder rejects documents

The county publishes two top ten lists of rejection reasons, and several repeat. In the Abstract department the usual causes are a missing well certificate or well statement, a missing drafting statement, no marital status, the wrong number for a document being satisfied or assigned, an incorrect recording fee, and a missing or half-finished CRV. Taxes that are not current also lead to a rejection.

Torrens filings face a stricter test. The legal description and owner names must match the certificate of title exactly, cross reference numbers must be right, and a bank name change needs an extra $20 memorial fee. Every document must also meet the standards in Minnesota Statutes section 507.093. A rejected package costs you days, and that hurts when the closing date is fixed.

Unpaid taxes and your deed

Delinquent taxes can block a deed. Section 272.12 requires the county auditor to check for delinquent tax when a deed is presented. The Recorder may not accept the deed without the auditor's note that no delinquent taxes are owed and the transfer is entered. Deeds of distribution in probate and transfer on death deeds are among the listed exceptions. Call Rice County Property Tax & Elections at 507-332-6104 for a current balance before you schedule closing.

Northfield crosses into Dakota County. A parcel in that part of town is not recorded in Rice County, so check the county on the tax statement before you send anything.

After the deed is recorded

The Recorder returns the original, and the title company or buyer arranges the next steps. Section 272.115 has the assessor drop homestead status on a sold property for the following year, unless the buyer applies and qualifies. Rice County has 25,596 housing units, so recorders see steady volume from sales. To see what is already recorded against your parcel, search LandShark or stop by the research area.

Research your parcel before listing

Three tools cover most of the checking. The county's Beacon site holds a searchable property tax map for every parcel. The Recorder's public research area in Faribault lets you pull the recorded history of your land during business hours without charge. LandShark gives subscribers remote access to the scanned images.

If your title history is long, a closing agent may order an abstract update, and a Torrens owner can ask the Registrar for the current certificate of title. Looking at the file early turns up old mortgages that were never released, easements, and legal description quirks that would otherwise hold up a closing. Sellers who plan a cash sale skip much of the lender-driven paperwork, but the deed itself still has to meet every item above, so the same checklist applies.

Frequently asked questions

How much is the recording fee for a deed in Rice County?

It is $46 for indexing and recording most instruments, set by Minnesota Statutes section 357.18. State deed tax is separate and goes on its own check.

Does Rice County accept electronic recording?

Yes. Simplifile, CSCGlobal, eRecording Partners, Indecomm Global Services and Hopdox are the e-recording partners. Call 507-332-6114 to learn which one suits your closing.

Can I look at Rice County land records for free?

Yes. The public research area at the Government Services Building in Faribault is open during business hours, and viewing is free. Copies cost $1.00 per page.

What is the Minnesota deed tax on a Rice County sale?

It is .0033 of the net consideration when that is above $3,000, and $1.65 when it is $3,000 or less. Payment comes with the deed when it is handed in.

Can the Rice County Recorder help me write a deed?

No. The office will not give legal advice or help prepare documents. Staff can explain filing requirements, and an attorney or your closing agent should draft the deed.

Who records deeds in Sherburne County

The Recorder's Office in Elk River keeps the land records for every parcel in the county. Deeds, mortgages and related filings all land there, and staff check each one for the required information before it goes on record.

Walk-in recording needs no appointment, although other services do. The office sits in the Government Center at 13880 Business Center Drive NW, Suite 100, Elk River, MN 55330-4668. Call 763-765-4420 with questions. Birth and death certificates come from the same counter, which can mean a line on busy days.

What happens after you hand over a deed

Most sellers never touch the filing. The county recommends eRecording for anyone who submits regularly and points to the Minnesota Land Title Association directory for firms that can send documents electronically. If you bring a paper deed yourself, expect these steps:

  1. Staff read it for completeness against state requirements.
  2. They confirm that the right fees came with it.
  3. It gets a sequential number and a date and time stamp.
  4. Clerks index it by legal description and by grantor and grantee, plus more than 20 other fields.
  5. Indexing is checked, then the page is scanned and the image reviewed.
  6. A receipt is prepared and the copy goes back to the presenter.

Two terms differ here. Recording means a reproduction goes back to you, and filing means the office retains the original. Staff can't draft a deed or advise you on one, under Minnesota Statutes 481.02. A real estate attorney is the right contact for drafting questions.

Why Sherburne County deeds get rejected

The recorder publishes the usual reasons a real estate document is sent back unrecorded. Walk through them before the closing date.

  • Back taxes remain unpaid on the parcel.
  • No draftsman statement.
  • Deed tax or mortgage registration tax computed wrongly.
  • A legal description that differs from the records, or looks doubtful.
  • A Certificate of Real Estate Value that is absent or half finished.
  • No mailing name and address for future tax statements.
  • A notary block with gaps.
  • A recording fee that is short or over.
  • Well information left off a transfer document.

Most of these are paperwork items that a title company checks routinely, which is a good reason to send the deed through one.

Recorder fees

The county collects no conservation fee. Deed tax, mortgage registration tax and the value certificate are handled at the Auditor/Treasurer's Office, so ask there for the amounts. A separate copy and use fee sheet took effect January 1, 2026, and charges $2.00 for page one of a mailed copy and $0.50 for each page after it.

Abstract or Torrens: which system covers my parcel?

Minnesota runs two land systems side by side, and both are recorded in this office. An abstract is a condensed history of every deed, mortgage and other document touching the land. A lender or buyer hires an attorney or title insurer to read that history and confirm the title is clear. Many Sherburne County abstracts begin with the recorded homestead documents.

Torrens works differently. A court orders a certificate of title, and that certificate is the title. The Recorder serves as Registrar of Titles under the District Court's control, with a court-appointed Examiner as adviser. Chapter 508 of Minnesota Statutes bars the Registrar from accepting certain instruments without the Examiner's certification or a court order. If you can't tell which system applies, call 763-765-4420 before a deed is drafted, since Torrens transfers carry their own fees.

Well information on a transfer document

A deed that needs a Certificate of Real Estate Value also needs well information. For a property with no wells, the document says so in a short statement, for example that the seller knows of no wells on the land.

A property with a well takes a completed Well Disclosure Certificate. A seller can skip a new certificate by stating that the number and status of wells match the last one filed. To find out whether one already exists, call the Minnesota Department of Health at 800-383-9808 or search its online well database.

Elk River is the county seat and largest city. The county had 104,194 people in mid-2025, up 7.2% from April 2020, and it issued 319 permits for new buildings in 2025.

Because so many homes are owner-occupied, most recorder traffic comes from ordinary sales, refinances and estates, and the staff see the same paperwork errors repeatedly.

Other recorder services during a sale

Property Watch is a free alert that contacts you by email or phone when a document is recorded under your name. The county also runs fee escrow accounts, with a $200 minimum balance, so a payment shortfall doesn't stall a recording.

  • State tax liens are indexed by taxpayer name, with a $30 fee at release, and federal liens and releases cost $46.
  • Completed foreclosure sales, court records and plat searches have links on the recorder's page.
  • The Sheriff holds foreclosure sales at the Government Center on Tuesdays and Wednesdays at 10 a.m.
  • A Sheriff's certificate of redemption costs $250 and requires a request 10 days or more ahead.

Tax statements are mailed in March, and a parcel's taxes turn delinquent after the payable year ends. Ask the Auditor/Treasurer at 763-765-4350 for the amount owed before you close.

State rules behind a Sherburne County closing

For any sale above $3,000, someone must file a certificate of value with the county auditor when the deed is recorded, as Minnesota Statutes 272.115 directs. The state deed tax is .0033 of net consideration, set by section 287.21.

After a sale, the assessor drops the homestead label for the next assessment year unless the new owner applies and qualifies.

Steps for a quick sale

Work backward from closing. Ask the Auditor/Treasurer for the tax balance, confirm whether the parcel is Abstract or Torrens, and decide who prepares the deed, since staff can't draft it. Gather the well information, the mailing name and address for future tax statements, and a completed Certificate of Real Estate Value. Then have a title company or attorney review the package against the rejection list above.

A listing adds showings and a buyer's loan. A cash sale skips those, but the recording steps and the tax and value paperwork stay the same. Sign up for Property Watch so you see the day the deed is recorded.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Anoka County?

Recorder's office and what it does

The Anoka County Recorder and Registrar of Titles, part of Property Records & Taxation, files deeds, mortgages and satisfactions and keeps the permanent archive of recorded real property documents. The office is at 2100 3rd Avenue, Anoka, MN 55303. Call 763-323-5400 with questions before you send a document, since a rejected filing costs you days at closing and sometimes a second round of fees.

Minnesota Statute 481.02 bars county staff from giving legal advice, helping prepare documents or performing abstracting. Staff send people who need help to a real estate attorney or a title company, and the county takes no liability for documents people complete themselves. The Land Records & Recording page has the details.

Abstract and Torrens property

Anoka County runs two parallel land record systems, as Minnesota law allows. Most parcels here are Abstract property, the traditional kind. When Abstract property sells, a thorough title search should look for any document that mentions the parcel.

Torrens property has a Certificate of Title that gives conclusive proof of ownership, with some exceptions, and it pulls the record into one document. Owners may convert property from Abstract to Torrens through land registration. If you do not know which system applies to your house, ask the recorder before the deed is drafted, because Torrens transfers carry their own certificate fees. Your closing agent will also want to know, since the title commitment, the recording steps and the final cost all differ between the two. A quick phone call to the recorder at the start of a sale is cheaper than a rejected deed at the end.

What a deed must include to be recorded

The county publishes a checklist on its recording requirements page. Read it top to bottom before anything goes in the mail.

  • The original document, dated and signed
  • A complete acknowledgment with the date, notary signature, legible seal and commission expiration date
  • Names and marital status of the people signing, and corporate details if a business signs
  • A complete legal description, with any exhibits noted and attached
  • A "Drafted by" line with name and address
  • Filing fees, with no white-out or white-out tape on any document
  • A "Send tax statements to" line naming the buyer
  • Payment in full of delinquent taxes, and of current-year taxes if the parcel is being split

Transfer deeds, including contracts for deed, also need a well disclosure. That can be a completed Well Disclosure Certificate with a $54 fee, or one of two sentences on the deed: either the seller knows of no wells, or the well status has not changed since the last filed certificate.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Anoka County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Recording fees and deed tax

These fees took effect July 1, 2025. Deed tax is the large item, and Minnesota Statute 287.21 sets it.

Selected Anoka County recording charges
ChargeAmount
Recording fee for an Abstract document$46.00
State deed tax on consideration above $3,0000.33% of net consideration
State deed tax at $3,000 or less$1.65
Agricultural conservation fee$5.00
Well certificate$54.00
Mortgage registration tax0.23% of debt secured
Certified copy of a document$10.00
Interested party fee, per parcel$15.00

The deed tax is due when the deed is presented for recording. Torrens filings have a separate fee list, such as $46 for a new Certificate of Title.

Mortgage paperwork has its own math. The mortgage registration tax is the amount of debt secured times 0.0023, plus the $5 conservation fee, and a mortgage paid in another county still owes the $5 in Anoka County. Satisfactions and assignments that cite four documents or fewer cost $46, with $10 more for each document cited beyond the fourth.

Certificate of real estate value

You need one for sales above $3,000, with a few exceptions. Minnesota Statute 272.115 requires the grantor, grantee or their agent to file a certificate of value when the deed is presented for recording. Anoka County wants the completed electronic certificate, called an eCRV, and its number on the transfer document.

The certificate lists the sale price, the property's classification and the financing terms. It carries the Social Security or employer number of each party, which the statute treats as private data. A filed certificate also keeps the buyer eligible for homestead status, since the statute bars homestead treatment for a sold property when none was filed. The assessor removes homestead status for the following year after a sale unless the buyer applies and qualifies.

How to submit a deed

There are three routes.

  • eRecording, which title companies, lenders and law firms use, through CSC eRecording Solutions, ePN, Indecomm and Simplifile.
  • Mail, with the documents and fees sent to Anoka County Property Records & Taxation at 2100 3rd Avenue, Anoka, MN 55303.
  • In person at the same address, paying by cash, check, debit or credit card, or Apple Pay.

If a title company is handling your closing, ask whether it will e-record the deed. If you are filing on your own, such as a transfer between relatives, send the signed original, the eCRV number, the well disclosure and a payment covering the deed tax and fees.

Plan the order of steps. Get the deed drafted by an attorney or title company, sign it in front of a notary, file the eCRV, attach the well disclosure, and then present everything with payment. The recorded deed becomes the permanent record, and certified copies cost $10.00 each if your lender or buyer asks for one. If any delinquent tax is owed on the parcel, it has to be paid before the deed can be recorded, so call the office early in the week of your closing.

Before you file, walk through the checklist above one more time. A missing notary seal or a blank "Send tax statements to" line is the usual reason a deed comes back, and a cash sale gets no shortcut here: the same paperwork and fees apply.

Local context

The county counts 381,605 residents across twenty cities, among them Blaine, Coon Rapids, Fridley and Andover. A deed for a house in any of those cities lands at this single county office, so there is no city-level recording desk to look for. About 90.7% of residents lived at the same address a year earlier, and owner-occupied median value is $346,500. The southeastern tip that was once Manomin County joined Anoka County in 1869, so very old deeds in that corner can carry unfamiliar place names.

Frequently asked questions

What is the recording fee for a deed in Anoka County?

It is $46.00 for an Abstract document under the schedule effective July 1, 2025. The state deed tax, the $5 agricultural conservation fee and a $54 well certificate fee come on top when they apply.

How much is the deed tax on an Anoka County sale?

It is 0.33% of net consideration when the price is above $3,000, and $1.65 when the price is $3,000 or less. The $5 conservation fee is added. The tax is due when the deed is presented for recording.

Does an Anoka County deed need well information?

Yes, every transfer deed and contract for deed does. Attach a Well Disclosure Certificate with its $54 fee, or put a qualifying statement on the deed that the seller knows of no wells or that the wells are unchanged.

Can I record an Anoka County deed online?

Yes, through eRecording submitters such as CSC eRecording Solutions, ePN, Indecomm or Simplifile. These services are meant for title companies, lenders and law firms, so an individual seller normally relies on the closing agent.

Will the Anoka County Recorder help me draft a deed?

No. The county gives no legal advice and does not help prepare documents or do abstracting. It recommends a real estate attorney or title company.
